title: Are You Fighting Lust… or Feeding It Quietly?
paragraphs:
Are You Fighting Lust… or Feeding It Quietly?
The Sin You Pray Against at Night but Entertain in Secret by Day
You closed the app… but not before looking one last time.

You told yourself it wasn’t that bad.
“It’s just a scroll.”
“It’s just curiosity.”
“It’s not like I acted on it.”

But something inside you went quiet afterward. Not peaceful… just quieter.
Like conviction got suffocated under justification.
And now here you are again… asking God for strength… while secretly keeping the door unlocked.
Be honest.
Are you really fighting lust… or just managing it well enough to keep your conscience calm?
Because Scripture doesn’t treat lust like a harmless thought—it exposes it like a fire already burning.
Jesus didn’t soften it. He intensified it.
In Matthew 5:28, He says:
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

The Greek word used here for “lustful intent” is ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō)—it doesn’t mean accidental attraction. It means a deep, consuming desire… a craving that lingers… a willful gaze that feeds the imagination.

This isn’t about noticing beauty.
This is about choosing to dwell on it… to replay it… to mentally possess what God never gave you.
And the part that should shake you is this:
Jesus says the sin isn’t waiting for the act.
It already happened in your heart.

That late-night scrolling?
That saved content?
That “just five seconds” look that turned into minutes?
That wasn’t harmless.
That was participation.
James writes it plainly in James 1:14–15:

Lust is not neutral.
It’s pregnant.
It doesn’t stay contained—it grows, it matures, it demands more.
And what started as a glance slowly becomes a grip.

You don’t fall into lust overnight.
You feed it… quietly… consistently… until it feels normal.
That’s the deception.

You can still pray.
Still worship.
Still show up at church.
But inside… something is dividing.
David knew this war intimately. A man after God’s own heart… yet still capable of falling hard.
In Psalm 51:10, after his sin with Bathsheba, he cries out:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”
The Hebrew word for “create” here is בָּרָא (bara)—the same word used in Genesis when God created the heavens and the earth.
David wasn’t asking for a small adjustment.
He was asking for a complete re-creation.
Because he understood something most people ignore:

You can’t manage lust.
You need God to remake your heart.
And yet… we try to control it instead of crucify it.

We negotiate with it.
We rename it.
We excuse it because “everyone struggles.”
But Scripture doesn’t say “cope with your flesh.”
It says in Galatians 5:24:
“And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.”
Crucified.

Not hidden.
Not reduced.
Not scheduled around your spiritual life.
Killed.
So ask yourself again… and don’t rush past it this time:
Are you starving your flesh… or feeding it just enough to keep it alive?
Because what you feed… grows.
And what you starve… dies.
This is where it gets uncomfortable.

Because you already know the places you go that weaken you.
You already know the triggers you refuse to cut off.
You already know the moments where you choose compromise instead of obedience.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:29:
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away.”
That’s not about self-harm—it’s about radical separation from sin.
It means if something leads you there… it has to go.

Not later.
Not when you feel stronger.
Now.
Because delayed obedience is still disobedience.
And the truth most people won’t say out loud is this:
Some of you aren’t trapped.
You’re tolerating it.
You don’t hate the sin… you just hate the guilt.
But there is still grace.
Not cheap grace that excuses… but powerful grace that transforms.
1 Corinthians 10:13 says:
“No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and He will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation He will also provide the way of escape…”
The Greek word for “escape” is ἔκβασις (ekbasis)—it means a way out… an exit route already prepared.
Which means every time you said “I couldn’t help it”… wasn’t fully true.
There was a door.
But you didn’t take it.
And this isn’t written to condemn you—it’s written to wake you up.
Because Jesus didn’t die so you could stay stuck in cycles you secretly protect.
He died to break them.
To cleanse you.
To restore what lust has been draining out of your soul.
Pause.
Let it sit.
Let it expose what you’ve been hiding—even from yourself.
And be honest… not polished, not religious… just real.
Your honesty could be the moment someone else realizes they’re not alone.
You’ll need to come back to it the next time temptation whispers louder than truth.
And if you truly want to glorify God—not just in words but in action—support what is feeding your spirit instead of what’s feeding your flesh.
You don’t overcome lust by trying harder.
You overcome it by surrendering deeper.
Because the same Jesus who saw your secret sin… still chose the cross for you.
And He’s not done rewriting your story.
The battle isn’t proof you’ve lost… it’s proof you’re still being pursued.
